You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The bug report describes an IOException triggered when writing a directory entry name that exceeds 100 bytes in a tar archive, specifically related to writing the PAX headers for the entry. The test case "testWriteNonAsciiDirectoryNamePosixMode" writes an entry with a non-ASCII directory name (containing ö characters) and enables the option to add PAX headers for non-ASCII names. This means the code path will generate PAX headers with the "path" attribute to store the name correctly.

Looking at the putArchiveEntry method, when the longFileMode is LONGFILE_POSIX, the code adds the entry name to the paxHeaders map with the key "path". Then, if addPaxHeadersForNonAsciiNames is true and the entry's name cannot be encoded in ASCII, it also puts the "path" attribute into the paxHeaders map. When paxHeaders has entries, writePaxHeaders is called.

In the writePaxHeaders method, a special PAX header entry named "./PaxHeaders.X/" plus a sanitized entry name is created. Notably, if this PAX header entry name length exceeds TarConstants.NAMELEN (usually 100), it is truncated to 99 characters. Then it prepares the header lines for each key-value pair, calculating and adjusting each line's length prefix to match the actual byte length of the line in UTF-8 encoding. Finally, it sets the size of the PAX header entry before calling putArchiveEntry(pex), writes the PAX header data, and closes the entry.

The exception in the bug report "request to write '114' bytes exceeds size in header of '0' bytes" is consistent with pex.setSize(data.length) not correctly setting the size before calling putArchiveEntry(pex), or with some subsequent call not updating the size.

However, in writePaxHeaders, before the recursive call to putArchiveEntry(pex), pex.setSize(data.length) is correctly called. So the size should not be 0 there.

One potential issue is recursive calls to putArchiveEntry inside writePaxHeaders could mishandle paxHeaders or longFileMode and re-enter paxHeaders writing or cause the size to be reset or miscalculated.

Also, in putArchiveEntry, when the header is written using entry.writeEntryHeader, it relies on the size set in the entry.

Another suspicious place is that in the paxHeaders key "path", the value might have more than 100 bytes, but the pax header entry name (the "name" variable in writePaxHeaders) is truncated to 99 characters, which may be insufficient to uniquely or correctly represent the PAX headers, potentially causing issues downstream.

Moreover, the longFileMode only handles the "path" attribute and does not handle the link name or other values passed in the PAX headers.

The root cause matches the bug report that long directory names cause an error in the pax header writing because the pax header entry is incorrectly truncating the name (the PAX header filename) or the size field is mismanaged leading to a zero size in the header.

The test triggers putArchiveEntry with a directory name with non-ASCII characters exceeding the 100 byte limit, forcing the addPaxHeadersForNonAsciiNames path. The pax header's name is truncated but may not be valid, resulting in a header size mismatch and IOException.

Recent bug reports about long names and modes handling errors with LONGFILE_GNU or POSIX support also align with this bug.

In summary:
- The putArchiveEntry method detects long names and prepares paxHeaders.
- writePaxHeaders creates a PAX header entry with a truncated name if too long.
- The pax header entry size is set before calling putArchiveEntry recursively.
- Despite this, the header ends up with a size of 0 or otherwise invalid, causing an IOException when writing the data.
- The truncation of the PAX header entry name or the recursive handling of putArchiveEntry inside writePaxHeaders is the likely cause.
- The test with a non-ASCII directory name triggers the problematic path.

Therefore, the bug is caused by writePaxHeaders truncating the PAX header entry name to 99 characters without ensuring uniqueness or correctness and recursive putArchiveEntry calls that possibly reset or mishandle the size field of the PAX header entry, leading to size mismatch exceptions.

The fix would be to ensure the PAX header entry name is formed correctly (perhaps with a better unique mapping rather than simple truncation) and that recursive calls to putArchiveEntry correctly handle the paxHeaders and size information to avoid zero size headers.

Suggested places to fix:
- TarArchiveOutputStream.putArchiveEntry
- TarArchiveOutputStream.writePaxHeaders

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
